messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
parts:
One of the common problems that we keep running into is that
everyone has different, and usually incomplete, understandings
of probability. Of course probability theory is relatively abstract
and we’re not going to be able to teach it to those without
reasonable math backgrounds: in that case the approaches
of McElreath and Kruschke are probably best. What doesn’t
exist in the literature is an introductory treatment of probability
theory and inference that goes into all of the technical details
for those who do have a reasonable math background. I’m
talking about concepts like concentration of measure, the
difference between probability, probability mass functions,
and probability density function.

Anyways, I think we’re going to need a treatment like that
in the Stan manual going forward, and this is my best
attempt at an initial draft, https://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro/blob/master/stan_intro.pdf.
Conditioned on a familiarity with calculus everything should,
hopefully, be self-contained and well-defined.

The inference section is still a little bit in flux, but I’m really
happy about the general organization of the probability sections.
That said, I’m sure there are many topics that unclear or
too hastily introduced or could use more examples to build
intuition, so let me have it. Either here on the list or via an
issue/PR. Otherwise let me know what you think.

messages.author: 49e107cb0f8a3d27
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
parts:
I looked it as well and think it’s excellent. It organizes a lot of ideas that I wish were presented this way more often (e.g., I really like section 5’s presentation on MAP estimators as dirac point mass approximations, Laplace estimators as the previous+covariance, variational estimators as optimization given a divergence function).

That said, I can’t tell how feasible this is for a person just getting into probability, even assuming the person has all the necessary mathematical background. It all seems too abstract to get a good handle of these objects as a first exposure. Joe Blitzstein and Carl Morris have an ongoing book manuscript on probability theory for statistical sciences that caters to the applied realm very well; they have several organizational techniques that might be useful here.

I like the separation of estimators into deterministic and stochastic; I also took a similar route as I’m writing this Python package that does statistical inference, and the internals use two base classes which correspond to these two paradigms. I wanted to mention one caveat, which is that the distinction can be quite blurry and it could be important to be mindful of these complications. As some examples which I’m sure you’re familiar with: a MAP optimization procedure with constant learning rate can converge with the target distribution as the stationary distribution; stochastic approximation theory uses Monte Carlo estimators within the steps to reach a stationary point and is not deterministic; and the expressiveness of the approximating family can grow unboundedly to indeed include the posterior as one such member in the family.

Dustin

Typically the material is presented as an abstract probability
triplet (sample space, sigma algebra, and probability distribution)
that doesn’t have any meaningful sense of value. Then random
variables map that system onto R or some R^{n} which does
have value, basically defining a “measurement” of the abstract
system. Then you go through all of the rigamarole of pushing
the sigma algebra and probability distribution forward onto
the image of the random variable to give a new probability
system you can actually calculate with using calculus. But
if you ignore all of the intermediate steps then all you’ve
done is changed representations (and maybe marginalized).

I never liked any of that as it’s never how things are done
operationally, hence my focus on equivalent sample spaces
as just being a representation degeneracy, which is ultimately
all it is.

> outcome, which are tightly coupled. If I understood what Michael

This is a slightly particular example — if you can partition a
sample space into sets then you can always construct a discrete
probabilistic system implicitly by the mass function with takes

p(x_{1}) = \mathbb{P} [ A_{1} ].

Kind of like a singular marginalization from a continuous space
into a discrete one.

As I noted in the original email, this is not meant as a gentle introduction
to people who want to learn about probability but don’t like math. In fact,
I _really_ don’t like trying to teach probability without some mathematical
foundation, because all it leads to is paradoxes and confusion!

What always happens is that people try to introduce probability theory
with probability densities and then inevitably everyone gets confused
with what are probabilities and what are densities and intuiting probability
as density and then becoming frustrated.

Or you could stick to probabilities over discrete spaces, but then you
don’t get to do anything on continuous spaces, which means no Gaussians
and other members of the exponential family.

This introduction is meant as the minimal material needed to really understand
statistical computation so that there are no “gotchya!”s that will bite the reader
later when they try to apply any lessons to real problems. Note that I went
to great effort to focus on concepts and relationships between concepts and
not on unhelpful calculation or proofs.

I am happy to add more examples and spend more time expositing on concepts
(suggestions, please!) At the same time, however, we have to be careful that
the reader doesn’t take the examples too seriously and lose some of the
necessary generality/abstraction.

One specific comment. You write

p(d|theta) as a function of d is conditional probability distribution.

p(d|theta) as a function of theta is the likelihood L(d|theta) which

probability distribution (posterior) and sometimes prior is required

explicit that we are making statements about parameters theta.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
parts:
p(d|theta) as a function of d is conditional probability distribution.

p(d|theta) as a function of theta is the likelihood L(d|theta) which
is not a probability distribution. Sometimes it's proportional to a
probability distribution (posterior) and sometimes prior is required
to make it possible to normalise the posterior.

This is not entirely true — any conditional probability distribution,
p[ E | theta ], is a probability distribution for any theta in the
second argument and a measurable function for any E in the
first argument.  They are mathematically the same object.

The distinction I think you are trying to get at is more subtle,
and involves not just the likelihood but also the marginal
likelihood.  When we update from the prior to the posterior
measure theoretically we need a function,

P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] = (dP^{post} / dP^{prior})(theta)  P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ]
P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] \equiv f(theta) P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ].

f is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the posterior with respect
to the prior, but is also the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the 
likelihood with respect to the marginal likelihood (this is basically
the measure theoretical version of Bayes’ Theorem).  

So the ambiguity that can arise is between the likelihood 
(a conditional probability distribution) and this updating
function (a Radon-Nikodym derivative).  But because you
need measure theory to make all of this make sense, and
it doesn’t really affect any practical use of Bayes, I don’t
think it’s all that helpful to discuss.

My thoughts about this have been influenced, e,g, by A. P. Dawid who has wrote the following

By A.P. Dawid
-------------------------------------------------------------------------

In a (doubtless ill-fated) attempt to explain more clearly the
essential distinction between a STATISTICAL MODEL and a LIKELIHOOD
FUNCTION --- one that until recently was widely understood but now
seems to engender great confusion --- I will try and make the point
as concrete as possible.

I am fishing. Everybody agrees that fish will bite according to a
Poisson process (hence the name!) of some rate \lambda bites per
hour. \lambda is unknown and we wish to make some inference about
\lambda from observing my performance.

Observer O1 plans to turn up after 3 hours and find out how many
fish, N, I have caught.

The STATISTICAL MODEL for N is the Poisson family Po(\lambda), with
discrete probability mass function:

(1) p_1( n | \lambda) = \exp{- 3 \lambda} \lambda^n /n!
(n = 0, 1, ...; \lambda >0 )

Observer O2 asks me to call her mobile as soon as I have caught 12
fishes. She will note the time T of this event.

The STATISTICAL MODEL for T is a Gamma family, Ga(12, \lambda),
with continuous probability density function:

(2) p_2( t | \lambda) = (\lambda^{12}/ 11!) t^{11} \exp{ -\lambda t}
(t > 0; \lambda > 0)

Now it so happens that I catch my 12th fish after exactly 3 hours.
Thus O1 observes N=12, while O2 observes T=3. Even though they
have ** utterly different ** STATISTICAL MODELS, involving even
different variables and different sample spaces, for this
particular outcome both O1 and O2 agree that the LIKELIHOOD
FUNCTION for \lambda (i.e. p_1( 12 | \lambda) for O1, p_2( 3 |
\lambda) for O2) is proportional to

(3) L(\lambda) = \lambda^{12} \exp{ -3 \lambda}
(\lambda > 0)

Indeed, I too Would obtain this, using as my STATISTICAL MODEL the
full Poisson process, and as my data the complete record of my
performance (i.e. exactly when each fish was caught) in the first 3
hours.

In no sense is (3) a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION for anything (or even
a probability for anything).

This example can be used to make various points about the
likelihood principle, optional stopping, sufficiency, etc. --- but
I will leave it there for now.

I surmise that one reason for the current confusion is the
(correct) statement that, in order to calculate a posterior
distribution we need both a prior distribution and a likelihood.
In fact it is only the ``observed'' likelihood function (e.g. (3)
in the story above) that is required. But typically we will have
started from a fully specified STATISTICAL MODEL, using this to
derive the relevant observed LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION. Because of this
link the distinction between the two has been elided.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
parts:
Phil is making the same mistake, conflating the likelihood
(a collection of probability distributions over data from a
frequentist perspective of a conditional probability distribution
from a Bayesian perspective) with the Radon-Nikodym
derivative that gets used in updating (what he calls the
“observed” likelihood).

The likelihood is a conditional probability distribution, so
if we plug in any data event then we get a function from
parameters to probabilities,

L[E_{D} | theta ] : theta \mapsto [0, 1].

But that’s not all that useful because we’ll mostly be
considering point events which have zero measure,
so this map degenerates to mapping everything to zero.

We could look at the corresponding conditional probability
density function l(d | theta), but then this depends on the
sample space. It’s why you get different density functions
if you’re looking at counts or time in Phil’s example.

When we’re performing a Bayesian update we care
about neither of these. We care only about the the
Radon-Nikodym derivative of the likelihood with respect

to the marginal likelihood,

f(d, theta) = dL_{conditional} / dL_{marginal} = l (d | theta} / l(d).

This is now a map from a point in data space and a parameter
to a real number, and we can plug in the observed data to
update our prior to our posterior,

P_{post} = f(d, theta) P_{prior}.

Now here’s the cool thing — f(d, theta) is invariant under
measurable maps. You can see this from the density
representation — the Jacobians cancel in the ratio. So
the actual learning is invariant to the sample space we
use to express the measurements, as it should be! This
is why in Phil’s example the “observed” likelihood was
invariant. But it’s really the observed likelihood/marginal
likelihood ratio that’s true invariant.

> frequentist perspective of a conditional probability distribution
> from a Bayesian perspective) with the Radon-Nikodym
> derivative that gets used in updating (what he calls the
> “observed” likelihood).
>
> The likelihood is a conditional probability distribution, so
> if we plug in any data event then we get a function from
> parameters to probabilities,
>
> L[E_{D} | theta ] : theta \mapsto [0, 1].
>
> But that’s not all that useful because we’ll mostly be
> considering point events which have zero measure,
> so this map degenerates to mapping everything to zero.
>
> We could look at the corresponding conditional probability
> density function l(d | theta), but then this depends on the
> sample space. It’s why you get different density functions
> if you’re looking at counts or time in Phil’s example.
>
> When we’re performing a Bayesian update we care
> about neither of these. We care only about the the
> Radon-Nikodym derivative of the likelihood with respect
> to the marginal likelihood,
>
> f(d, theta) = dL_{conditional} / dL_{marginal} = l (d | theta} / l(d).
>
> This is now a map from a point in data space and a parameter
> to a real number, and we can plug in the observed data to
> update our prior to our posterior,
>
> P_{post} = f(d, theta) P_{prior}.
>
> Now here’s the cool thing — f(d, theta) is invariant under
> measurable maps. You can see this from the density
> representation — the Jacobians cancel in the ratio. So
> the actual learning is invariant to the sample space we
> use to express the measurements, as it should be! This
> is why in Phil’s example the “observed” likelihood was
> invariant. But it’s really the observed likelihood/marginal
> likelihood ratio that’s true invariant.
>

> > My thoughts about this have been influenced, e,g, by A. P. Dawid who has wrote the following

> > By A.P. Dawid
> > -------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >
> > In a (doubtless ill-fated) attempt to explain more clearly the
> > essential distinction between a STATISTICAL MODEL and a LIKELIHOOD
> > FUNCTION --- one that until recently was widely understood but now
> > seems to engender great confusion --- I will try and make the point
> > as concrete as possible.
> >
> > I am fishing. Everybody agrees that fish will bite according to a
> > Poisson process (hence the name!) of some rate \lambda bites per
> > hour. \lambda is unknown and we wish to make some inference about
> > \lambda from observing my performance.
> >
> > Observer O1 plans to turn up after 3 hours and find out how many
> > fish, N, I have caught.
> >
> > The STATISTICAL MODEL for N is the Poisson family Po(\lambda), with
> > discrete probability mass function:
> >
> > (1) p_1( n | \lambda) = \exp{- 3 \lambda} \lambda^n /n!
> > (n = 0, 1, ...; \lambda >0 )
> >
> > Observer O2 asks me to call her mobile as soon as I have caught 12
> > fishes. She will note the time T of this event.
> >
> > The STATISTICAL MODEL for T is a Gamma family, Ga(12, \lambda),
> > with continuous probability density function:
> >
> > (2) p_2( t | \lambda) = (\lambda^{12}/ 11!) t^{11} \exp{ -\lambda t}
> > (t > 0; \lambda > 0)
> >
> > Now it so happens that I catch my 12th fish after exactly 3 hours.
> > Thus O1 observes N=12, while O2 observes T=3. Even though they
> > have ** utterly different ** STATISTICAL MODELS, involving even
> > different variables and different sample spaces, for this
> > particular outcome both O1 and O2 agree that the LIKELIHOOD
> > FUNCTION for \lambda (i.e. p_1( 12 | \lambda) for O1, p_2( 3 |
> > \lambda) for O2) is proportional to
> >
> > (3) L(\lambda) = \lambda^{12} \exp{ -3 \lambda}
> > (\lambda > 0)
> >
> > Indeed, I too Would obtain this, using as my STATISTICAL MODEL the
> > full Poisson process, and as my data the complete record of my
> > performance (i.e. exactly when each fish was caught) in the first 3
> > hours.
> >
> > In no sense is (3) a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION for anything (or even
> > a probability for anything).
> >
> > This example can be used to make various points about the
> > likelihood principle, optional stopping, sufficiency, etc. --- but
> > I will leave it there for now.
> >
> > I surmise that one reason for the current confusion is the
> > (correct) statement that, in order to calculate a posterior
> > distribution we need both a prior distribution and a likelihood.
> > In fact it is only the ``observed'' likelihood function (e.g. (3)
> > in the story above) that is required. But typically we will have
> > started from a fully specified STATISTICAL MODEL, using this to
> > derive the relevant observed LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION. Because of this
> > link the distinction between the two has been elided.
> >
> > Phil
> >

> > A. P. Dawid, Professor of Statistics, Department of Statistical Science,
> > University College London, Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT, United Kingdom.

> >
> > On Friday, April 1, 2016 at 9:26:03 PM UTC+3, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >> p(d|theta) as a function of d is conditional probability distribution.
> >>
> >> p(d|theta) as a function of theta is the likelihood L(d|theta) which
> >> is not a probability distribution. Sometimes it's proportional to a
> >> probability distribution (posterior) and sometimes prior is required
> >> to make it possible to normalise the posterior.
> >>
> >> This is not entirely true — any conditional probability distribution,
> >> p[ E | theta ], is a probability distribution for any theta in the
> >> second argument and a measurable function for any E in the
> >> first argument. They are mathematically the same object.
> >>
> >>
> >> The distinction I think you are trying to get at is more subtle,
> >> and involves not just the likelihood but also the marginal
> >> likelihood. When we update from the prior to the posterior
> >> measure theoretically we need a function,
> >>
> >>
> >> P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] = (dP^{post} / dP^{prior})(theta) P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ]
> >> P^{post} [E_{Theta} | d ] \equiv f(theta) P^{prior} [ E_{Theta} ].
> >>
> >>
> >> f is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the posterior with respect
> >> to the prior, but is also the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the
> >> likelihood with respect to the marginal likelihood (this is basically
> >> the measure theoretical version of Bayes’ Theorem).
> >>
> >>
> >> So the ambiguity that can arise is between the likelihood
> >> (a conditional probability distribution) and this updating
> >> function (a Radon-Nikodym derivative). But because you
> >> need measure theory to make all of this make sense, and
> >> it doesn’t really affect any practical use of Bayes, I don’t
> >> think it’s all that helpful to discuss.

Okay, hopefully the last big change has been pushed: http://github.com/betanalpha/stan_intro.

The biggest change was an expanded discussion of propositional logic that completely
motivates measure and probability theory. Ultimately this is an introduction to measure/
probability theory, only without the usually mathematical pedantry and a much stronger
motivation from logic as a means of describing arbitrary systems. I also set up the
measure-theoretic version of Bayes’ Theorem from the beginning, again motivated
by logic, which makes the construction of Bayesian inference super easy.

I’m sure some of the notation can be cleaned up, and I’m happy to add more exposition
(or even exercises at some point?) if anyone finds sections particularly esoteric or
hard to read, but overall I think this is the level of detail that is necessary to really
understand what’s going on.

Once again, any and all comments are welcome.

messages.subject: Re: Draft for Technical Introduction to Probability for Stan
parts:
Thank you creating this technical introduction: very stimulating and enlightening!

I find section 4 challenging, so I'm sharing my thoughts in the hope of getting some clarification, and pointing out a concept other readers might struggle with. I am having a hard time with Concentration of Measure, particularly the fact the neighborhood we want to explore does not include the mode in the hyper-sphere example.

So here's what I get: the volume element is proportional to r^(D-1), so dV increases as we move away from the origin, which is where the mode is. Consequently, the PMF is NOT concentrated at the origin but at a certain shell. This is clearly illustrated in figure 4.2 (I would consider rewriting the equations for dV and PDF in the figure's description). From a "markov chain point of view" this is telling me that the vast majority of the parameters I want to include in my sample are located in the "typical set shell". If I only stick around the mode, I will get the parameters with the highest PDF, but most of the mass will be lost, and my final sample will be unrepresentative.

Ok -- so if I were to pick the most "massive" shell, it would certainly not be located at the origin. But why am I constrained to pick a shell? If instead of picking a shell, I were picking a finite volume to do my exploration in, wouldn't the most massive volume include the origin of the sphere (and maybe part of the typical set shell)? So the key question is why do I need to pick a shell, instead of a volume, which to me is what only exploring the typical set seems to imply.

My tentative answer is that it takes computational power for a markov chain to move around the parameter space. But I am then unsure how exploring the entire typical set shell ends up being less costly than moving to the center of the sphere and out of it again.

Any clarification would be welcome!

~ Charles

parts:
You’re not picking a single shell, you’re trying to understand where
in parameter space you should be evaluating the target function.
Any evaluations near the mode don’t contribute to any expectation
and so are wasted. You are welcome to include them, but will
pay a significant computational cost to do so.
